rv.q: Yes, it is bombastic and overwrought. It’s true that there’s enough smoke to make three Whitesnake videos. OK, it sometimes makes "The Phantom of the Opera" seem small and staid.
But for all the production’s excesses, it proves decidedly underwhelming, devoid of thrills or genuine emotion.

Unfortunately there’s no way to digitally airbrush away the hokum that pervades the whole show, like the ample stage smoke puffing away throughout the proceedings, giving a most commendable featured performance as the fabled pea-soupy London fog.
But the drab revival of Frank Wildhorn’s show that opened last night mucks it up.
Any performance of Frank Wildhorn and Leslie Bricusse’s horror show, mind, could correctly be described as limited...

No matter who's doing it or where it's being done, "Jekyll & Hyde" is still tuneless and tiresome, a musical for those who prefer power ballads to show tunes but find "The Phantom of the Opera" too challenging.
Either way, “Jekyll & Hyde” is an over-the-top bloody hoot.
Many of the same charms and flaws of the theme restaurants that dot the surrounding neighborhood are present in the production, and unfortunately the drinks are just as expensive.
Alas, a few glimpses of unfettered emotion cannot sustain a two-hour-plus parade of shrill melodrama.
''In each of us there are two natures,'' whispers a disembodied voice in the prologue to Frank Wildhorn's Jekyll & Hyde.
He and the rest of the cast, as directed and choreographed by Jeff Calhoun, have survived 25 weeks on tour.
Obviously, those were patrons unconcerned with being in the dramatic moment, and that is undoubtedly the audience for “Jekyll & Hyde.”

Ponytailed Jekyll and wild-haired Hyde are both played by Constantine Maroulis this time around, which would be reason enough to stay home — if Frank Wildhorn’s music and Leslie Briscusse’s book and lyrics didn’t already provide ample motivation to do that.
The new production does nothing to enhance the musical’s reputation.
Calhoun makes many unfortunate choices, including over-stressing the score's rock elements and using both nauseating video graphics and violent sexual imagery.
It's like being trapped at an audition for 'American Idol'.
Director Jeff Calhoun stages and choreographs the musical with no-holds-barred bravado that results in a fiendishly entertaining show.

cn.t: Critics largely pan this bombastic revival as overwrought and simplistic, drowning in smoke and power ballads, though some find campy entertainment value in its no-holds-barred excess and Maroulis's committed performance.

sg.ra: Closest and most direct view of the stage at Marquis Theatre, with the fullest sound. The standard top pick for any show here.
An elevated, full-stage view with no orchestra-level neck-craning — especially strong for shows with big staging or choreography.
A modest side angle on the stage but still close and clear — a reliable choice when center seats are sold out.
Farther from the stage than center orchestra — less up-close, but the sound still carries well.
At 1,611 seats, Marquis Theatre is one of the larger Broadway houses — far side mezzanine seats sit well off-axis and a long way from the stage.

vs.sum: The Marquis Theatre offers excellent comfort with spacious seating and good sightlines from most areas, although the ambiance is somewhat lacking due to its modern, hotel-integrated design. Facilities are well-equipped with ample restrooms and concessions, making it a convenient choice for theatergoers.

acc.note: Elevator via Marriott Marquis hotel. 10 wheelchair spaces. No elevator to Mezzanine.
